title: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture
subtitle: Defining unicast, multicast, and anycast address types for IPv6

eli5.summary: IPv6 addresses are very long numbers, and this document says how they are built, what kinds exist and how to write them down. Some are for one computer, some for a group, and some for the closest member of a group.

questions: how do you shorten an ipv6 address
what is the difference between unicast anycast and multicast

tldr.problem: IPv4's 32-bit addresses were running out, and a bigger address needed clear rules for its format, types and text form.
tldr.mechanism: 128-bit addresses whose leading bits give the type (unicast, anycast or multicast), written as hex groups with :: compression.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 hosts get a link-local address with no configuration and can use multicast instead of broadcast.

today: Every operating system with IPv6 turned on follows this architecture. Each interface automatically gets an fe80::/10 link-local address, and neighbor discovery and many local services use ff02:: multicast groups. RFC 4291 is the current base specification, and it has been updated by later RFCs (for example RFC 5952 for a recommended text form).

hero.subtitle: Defining unicast, multicast, and anycast address types for IPv6

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines the addressing architecture of the IP Version 6 (IPv6) protocol. It includes the IPv6 address format, the various types of addresses, and the rules for text representation of addresses.

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long. The address space is divided into multiple types based on the high-order bits, providing a structured and extensible addressing hierarchy.
sections.eli5: An IPv6 address is a very long number that says where a computer lives on the network. This document is the rule book for how those numbers are shaped and written down.

sections.title: Address Types
sections.content:
IPv6 defines three types of addresses. Unlike IPv4, there is no broadcast address in IPv6; its function is superseded by multicast.

Unicast
An identifier for a single interface. A packet sent to a unicast address is delivered to the interface identified by that address.
Anycast
An identifier for a set of interfaces (typically on different nodes). A packet sent to an anycast address is delivered to the nearest interface, as determined by routing protocol metrics.
Multicast
An identifier for a set of interfaces. A packet sent to a multicast address is delivered to all interfaces identified by that address.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of address. One goes to a single computer, one goes to the closest of a group, and one goes to everyone in a group.

sections.title: Text Representation
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are written as eight groups of one to four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. Several compression rules simplify the notation:

Address Compression Rules
Full form:       2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001
Leading zeros:   2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1
Consecutive ::   2001:db8::1

IPv4-mapped:     ::ffff:192.168.1.1
Loopback:        ::1
Unspecified:     ::

The :: notation can only be used once in an address to avoid ambiguity. For example, 2001:db8::1::2 is invalid because the parser cannot determine how many zero groups each :: represents.
sections.eli5: The long number is hard to write, so there are shortcuts: drop the extra zeros, and squeeze one long run of zeros into two colons.

sections.title: Unicast Addresses
sections.content:
IPv6 unicast addresses come in several forms, each serving a different purpose in the network architecture.

Global UnicastEverything not listed below. Globally routable, equivalent to IPv4 public addresses (currently allocated from 2000::/3)Any other prefix
Link-Localfe80::/10 - Valid only on a single linkPrefix: 1111 1110 10
Unique Localfc00::/7 - Private addresses, similar to RFC 1918 (defined in RFC 4193, not in this document)Prefix: 1111 110
Loopback::1 - Equivalent to IPv4 127.0.0.1128 bits
Unspecified:: - Indicates absence of an address128 bits
sections.eli5: Some addresses work anywhere in the world, some only on your own street, and a few are special, like "me" and "nobody yet".

sections.title: Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
Multicast addresses have the prefix ff00::/8. The flags and scope fields allow fine-grained control over multicast behavior.

ff02::1All nodes on the local link
ff02::2All routers on the local link
ff02::1:ff00:0/104Solicited-node multicast
ff05::2All routers in the site
sections.eli5: A multicast address is like a group chat name. The first few characters say how far the message may travel, and the rest names the group.

sections.title: Required Addresses
sections.content:
Every IPv6 node must recognize certain addresses to participate in the network.

Node Type
Required Addresses
Host
Link-local for each interface, loopback (::1), all-nodes multicast (ff02::1), solicited-node multicast for each unicast/anycast address
Router
All host-required addresses plus all-routers multicast (ff02::2) and subnet-router anycast for each interface

Every IPv6 interface must have at least one link-local address, and a node must recognize it as its own. In practice it is usually generated automatically from the interface identifier, so basic local connectivity works without manual configuration or DHCP.
sections.eli5: Every computer has to answer to a few built-in names, so it can say hello to its neighbors before anyone has set anything up.

data.title: IPv6 address examples
data.code:
2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334   full form, eight 16-bit groups
fe80::1%eth0                              link-local, with a zone (interface) suffix
::ffff:192.0.2.1                          IPv4-mapped address
ff02::1                                   all nodes on the local link

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: Binary 11111111 (ff) marks the address as multicast.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Four flags 0|R|P|T. The high-order flag is reserved and must be 0. T=0 means a permanently assigned (well-known) group; T=1 means a transient one. P is defined in RFC 3306 and R in RFC 3956.

fields.name: Scope
fields.desc: Limits how far the group reaches. 1 = interface-local, 2 = link-local, 5 = site-local, 8 = organization-local, E = global.

fields.name: Group ID
fields.desc: Identifies the multicast group, either permanent or transient, within the given scope.

items.title: Unicast
items.text: One interface. The packet goes to that one place.

items.title: Anycast
items.text: A set of interfaces. The packet goes to the nearest member.

items.title: Multicast
items.text: A set of interfaces. The packet goes to every member.

items.title: No broadcast
items.text: IPv6 has no broadcast address. Multicast takes over that job.
